Toyota Sequoia Enters MY27 With Trailhunter Package, TRD Pro Suspension Upgrade
20 photos
Photo: Toyota
Toyota has found another way to sell off-road capability without forcing customers into an expensive trim. For model year 2027, the Sequoia full-size hybrid sport utility vehicle gains a Trailhunter-branded package for the SR5 grade. Said package adds $3,500 to the final price, making it a very different proposition from the overly expensive TRD Pro specification.
If you ask me, Toyota knows what it's doing here. The SR5 Trailhunter and TRD Pro target customers with different preferences, and giving them choices is the best way of making the Sequoia more relevant in this particular segment. SR5 Trailhunter customers get Old Man Emu suspension, underbody protection, front recovery hooks, Michelin LTX Trail rubber boots, exclusive bronze wheels for said tires, and Trailhunter badging where it matters.
Crawl Control, Multi-Terrain Select, and a locking rear differential are on the menu as well, managing traction over a variety of surfaces. Unfortunately, this package is not compatible with the SR5 Premium package. Why? Beats me, but I do know that prospective customers are missing out on leather-trimmed seats.
At the other end of the spectrum, the TRD Pro takes a different route. For 2027, its maker gave it FOX QS3 adjustable shock absorbers. Red tow hooks and a new Honeycomb signature paint color pretty much complete the model year changes. Of course, ISO-dynamic seats and BBS forged wheels are on the menu as well.
All grades retain the familiar i-FORCE MAX twin-turbo V6 hybrid powertrain, which outputs a combined 437 horsepower and 583 pound-feet (790 Newton-meters) of twist. Being a hybrid, the electric side of the powertrain is especially useful in scenarios where near-instant torque delivery is preferred.
Photo: Toyota The hybrid oomph further enables a maximum towing capacity of 9,520 pounds (4,318 kilograms) when properly equipped for this kind of work. Speaking of towing, 2027 models get a more sophisticated group of trailer assistance tech. Automated Trailer Detection uses radar and the rear camera to detect a connected trailer, estimating its physical characteristics.
Trailer Blind Spot Monitor, Trailer Lane Trace Assist, and Trailer Backup Guide are highlights in their own right. While said features won't make towing completely foolproof, they address the less enjoyable parts of handling a large trailer. Toyota further worked its magic inside, where 14-inch touchscreen infotainment becomes standard across the board.
The instrument cluster is a 12.3-inch unit, and 5G connectivity is handled by AT&T. A built-in Drive Recorder Dash Cam also needs mentioning, for it uses exterior cameras to capture 20-second clips of automatically triggered or manual events. Footage can be reviewed on the center display.
Over-the-air software updates are on the menu as well, as is the Advanced Rear Seat Reminder that detects second- and third-row movement via millimeter-wave radar. When it comes to pricing, Toyota wants $69,900 for the most basic SR5 there is for model year 2027.
Add $2,195 for the destination fee, and you get $72,095 from the outset. Four-wheel drive is now standard, though. The first units should hit dealers this fall.
